source.title: Convolutional Nets Versus Vision Transformers for Diabetic Foot Ulcer Classification
source.authors: Adrian Galdran; Gustavo Carneiro; Miguel A. González Ballester

record.tranche_reason: Reports held-out classification performance for different architectures and for SGD versus SAM, using a different task and measures from the mapped claim versions. It does not report training error or train-test gaps.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation-set metrics for SGD and SAM and final-test metrics for four architectures. These results concern held-out performance, but the paper gives no training error, random-label fit, or train-test gap. Its CNN comparison is against vision transformers, not fully connected networks; SAM is not an adaptive optimizer; and it does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.test_reason: The study compares pretrained CNNs with vision transformers and SGD with SAM on diabetic-foot-ulcer classification. Neither comparison tests V1–V8: transformers are not fully connected comparators trained from scratch, SAM with SGD is not an adaptive-optimizer comparison, and optimizing sharpness does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or its correlation with generalization gaps.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors: they conclude that SAM improves performance for all considered models and CNNs may remain preferable in few-data scenarios. Their characterization of improvement as noticeable for every model is stronger than DeiT's 0.11-point F1 increase warrants without uncertainty estimates. Their broader statement that CNNs are always superior is also not true across all table metrics.
record.recipe_differences: Pretrained CNN and vision-transformer models are compared on diabetic-foot-ulcer classification; the optimizer comparison is SGD versus SAM, rather than the mapped adaptive-optimizer comparisons. Training also uses augmentation, repeated learning-rate cycles, and ensembling across data folds.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer choice changes validation metrics; architecture choice changes final-test metrics. The paper also states that SAM requires two forward passes per weight update.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM with SGD as its base optimizer yields higher reported validation metrics than standard SGD for all four architectures. Macro F1 increases from 51.34 to 57.71 for BiT-ResNeXt50, 47.55 to 57.65 for EfficientNet B3, 48.84 to 51.94 for ViT, and 53.87 to 53.98 for DeiT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM can improve held-out classification performance relative to SGD for pretrained CNNs and vision transformers on DFUC; improvement size depends on architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Final-test macro F1 is 61.53 for BiT-ResNeXt50, 59.71 for EfficientNet B3, 58.48 for ViT, and 57.29 for DeiT. The two CNNs outperform the two transformers on F1, although EfficientNet does not outperform both transformers on every metric.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ImageNet-pretrained CNNs can outperform ImageNet-pretrained vision transformers on macro F1 when fine-tuned on a small medical-image dataset.

record.problems: No training errors or train-test gaps are reported, so the measurements do not establish changes in generalization gap. Models start from ImageNet-pretrained weights, and the tested data are a single medical image classification task. The text reports no uncertainty estimates for these tables.
record.rows_left_out: none; 48 rows retained, one for each separately reported model, condition, and metric in Tables 1 and 2.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-versus-random-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and training recipe.
Width scaling beyond zero training error and its effect on test error.
CNN versus fully connected networks trained from scratch; contributions of local connectivity, learned sparsity, and convolutional initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, and optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and changes that remove their penalty; batch size is fixed at 32.
Effects of adding, removing, or varying dropout, including interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with train-test gaps, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and subsequent test accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: All 48 extracted metric values match Tables 1–2; their existing version links and states are appropriate. These rows describe method performance outside V1–V8 and supply no verdict evidence for those versions. Predictions are averaged across four training folds and test-time flips. No training losses, train-test gaps, or uncertainty estimates are reported. Table 1 prints EfficientNet's F1 difference as 10.05, but its endpoint values imply 10.10; the extracted endpoints are correct. Table 3's challenge ensemble and competitor scores are outside the versions and do not require missing-result entries.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Width scaling beyond interpolation and resulting test-error changes.
Comparison against fully connected networks, local connectivity, and the stated initialization or sparse-connection conditions.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD under the tuning conditions described.
Batch-size comparisons and the effect of epoch budgets or adapting training recipes.
Dropout addition or removal and its effect on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance and its relationship to train-test gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
